title: Effects of conditioned medium, secretome, and extracellular vesicles derived from human dental pulp stem cells on cancer cell behavior: A scoping review of preclinical evidence
html: ABSTRACT Objective To map preclinical evidence on the effects of conditioned medium (CM), secretome, and extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from human dental pulp stem/stromal cells on cancer cell behavior, including experimental models, biological outcomes, molecular findings, and knowledge gaps. Design This scoping review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and the PRISMA-ScR guideline. Six databases and Google Scholar were searched through July 3, 2026, supplemented by backward citation searching. Original preclinical studies evaluating DPSC-derived acellular products in experimental cancer models were included. Two reviewers independently selected studies and extracted data; findings were synthesized narratively. Results Thirteen publications representing twelve experimental datasets were included, although possible overlap between two reports remained unresolved. CM predominated, followed by EVs and stimulated secretome. Responses varied across models, including reduced viability, increased apoptosis, and impaired migration or invasion, alongside tumor-promoting or neutral findings. Two heterogeneous thyroid-cancer EV studies reported reduced invasion without significant cytotoxicity under the tested conditions; this preliminary pattern cannot be generalized. Molecular findings included JNK/ERK-associated signaling, caspase activation, Wnt-related expression, VEGF regulation, receptor-related changes, and extracellular matrix remodeling, predominantly without causal validation. Product characterization, methodological reporting, and independent replication were limited; direct in vivo evidence was scarce. Conclusions These preparations exhibit context-dependent biological activity, but current evidence does not establish therapeutic efficacy or oncological safety. Standardized preparation and characterization, independent replication, causal mechanistic validation, and rigorous in vivo investigation are required before clinical translation.
